title: Healing Wounds from the Past
shortDescription: Some wounds belong to the past, yet they still influence the way we think, react, and relate to others today. This five-day journey will help you recognize what still hurts, understand how those experiences continue to affect your present, bring them honestly before God, renew interpretations born from fear, and begin to walk with greater freedom without denying what you lived through.
learning: Recognize wounds from the past that still influence thoughts, emotions, and relationships
Understand how an old experience can continue shaping present reactions
Learn to bring pain before God without minimizing it or turning it into your identity
Identify thoughts and conclusions that need to be renewed by biblical truth
Develop a freer way to move forward without being defined by what you lived through
gains: Greater clarity about wounds that still need attention and healing
Less confusion between what happened and what is still true today
A more honest relationship with God regarding pain from the past
Tools to respond to the present without automatically repeating old defenses
Greater inner freedom to move forward with wisdom, hope, and a renewed identity

days.title: Recognize What Still Hurts
days.text:
There are wounds we learn to hide so well that we begin to think they no longer exist. We keep working, serving, smiling, and fulfilling responsibilities, yet certain words, places, or situations still awaken intense reactions. The past may have ended on the calendar, but it does not always end within the heart.

The Bible does not present healing as denial. The psalmist speaks of a God who heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. That image acknowledges that real harm occurred and that it needs care. Guarding the heart does not mean locking it away so no one can ever touch it again, but paying attention to what still lives within it.

Healing begins with honesty. You do not need to compare your pain with anyone else's or justify why it still affects you. What matters is acknowledging it before God. A wound that can be named can also begin to be cared for.
days.internalize: Write simply: “This still hurts because…”. Do not try to solve it yet. The first step is to acknowledge it without shame.
days.prayer: Lord, You know the wounds I still carry. Help me recognize them without hiding and trust that I can bring them before You. Draw near to what is still tender in my heart and begin your work of healing. Amen.
days.action: Identify one experience from the past that still produces a strong reaction in you. In one sentence, describe what happened, and in another, describe how it affects you today.

days.title: When the Past Keeps Interpreting the Present
days.text:
An old wound can become a filter. After being betrayed, we may interpret any delay as deception. After being rejected, a small criticism may feel like confirmation that we are not enough. After a controlling relationship, even an innocent question may feel threatening.

The problem is not remembering what we learned. Experience can give us wisdom. The problem arises when a past experience is given authority to automatically interpret every new situation. Then we are no longer responding only to what is happening today; we are also responding to something that happened long ago.

Paul speaks about renewing the mind and taking thoughts captive to the obedience of Christ. Part of healing is learning to pause before assuming. We can ask, “What is actually happening right now?” and distinguish it from what we fear might happen again. That pause opens space for freer and fairer responses.
days.internalize: Make this distinction: “what this person or situation is showing today” and “what my history fears may happen again.”
days.prayer: Father, show me when I am interpreting the present through old wounds. Renew my mind and give me discernment to recognize real risks without living ruled by memories and fears. Amen.
days.action: Think of a recent reaction that was very intense. Write down what actually happened in the present and what past experience may have influenced your interpretation.

days.title: Bring to God the Story You Cannot Change
days.text:
One of the hardest parts of healing is accepting that the past cannot be edited. We cannot change what someone said, recover certain years, or go back and make a different decision. That powerlessness can feed sadness, anger, or a constant need to imagine what life would have been like if something had happened differently.

The Psalms teach us to pour out our hearts before God. Prayer does not change the facts of the past, but it can change the way we carry them. Bringing a story to God means no longer managing it entirely on our own and allowing him into what still feels like a loss, an injustice, or an unresolved question.

There are moments when healing does not mean understanding why something happened. It means learning to say, “This is part of my story, but I do not want to keep carrying it without You.” Prayer then becomes a place where pain is no longer isolated.
days.internalize: You do not need to find an explanation for everything today. It may be enough to say: “Lord, I cannot change this, but I can stop carrying it alone.”
days.prayer: God, I place before You the part of my story I cannot change. You know what I lost, what I did not understand, and what still weighs on me. Help me surrender this burden to You and walk with You from here. Amen.
days.action: Write a prayer about something from the past that you cannot change. End with a specific sentence of surrender: “Today I place in your hands…”.

days.title: You Are Not the Same Person Who Survived That Wound
days.text:
Wounds can freeze an image of ourselves. We may continue seeing ourselves as the helpless, rejected, betrayed, or confused person we were at that moment. But even if the memory remains, we do not remain exactly the same.

Scripture speaks of renewal, new creation, and new paths. This does not mean a difficult experience disappears from our story, but that God can form in us abilities we did not have before: greater discernment, clearer boundaries, deeper maturity, and an identity less dependent on what others did.

Healing also means recognizing growth. Perhaps today you can say no where you once stayed silent, ask for help where you once isolated yourself, or recognize warning signs you once ignored. Those differences matter. The past explains some wounds, but it does not have authority to define everything you can become.
days.internalize: Complete this sentence: “Today I am not the same person I was then, because now I have learned…”.
days.prayer: Lord, help me recognize the work You have already done in me. Do not let me keep seeing myself only through the most wounded version of my story. Renew my identity and continue forming wisdom, strength, and hope in me. Amen.
days.action: Write down three specific ways you have grown since that experience: a way of thinking, a boundary, a decision, or an ability you now have.

days.title: Move Forward Without Denying Where You Came From
days.text:
Healing does not mean reaching a point where you never remember, never hurt, or never feel afraid again. It means the past no longer has authority to direct every decision. You can remember without living trapped and learn without building your whole life around the wound.

Paul speaks of reaching toward what lies ahead. Psalm 126 acknowledges tears and, at the same time, hope for fruit. Galatians calls us to stand firm in freedom. Together, these passages show a life that does not deny what was lived through but also does not remain stopped there.

Moving forward can be a slow process. Sometimes it will look like a different conversation, a new boundary, a healthier relationship, or a decision you would not have dared to make before. What matters is not erasing the past, but allowing God to have more authority over your present and future than what wounded you.
days.internalize: Close this journey with a truth: “My past explains part of my story, but it does not have permission to completely write what comes next.”
days.prayer: Jesus, thank you that my story does not end with my wounds. Help me remember without becoming trapped, learn without becoming hardened, and move forward in freedom. Let your work in me have more authority than what harmed me. Amen.
days.action: Write one next step for your healing over the next two weeks: a conversation, a boundary, a prayer practice, asking for support, or a specific decision that will help you move forward.
